div1.p: This is a mockup of an introduction to the undated letters.

div3.bibl:
Undated “I am not to get to Addiscombe on Sunday” Ashburton, Harriet Lady Ashburton, Harriet Lady
Thomas Carlyle
Harriet Lady Ashburton >
TC HARRIET LADY ASHBURTON
div3.sourceNote: TC-LA, n.d. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Dated not after 1855 because of TC’s mention of dinner with Samuel Rogers (1763–1855; ODNB)
div3.head: TC TO HARRIET LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: I am not to get to Addiscombe on Sunday; the amount of my sins is too heavy. I meditated a great feat for Sunday: coming out to breakfast with you, by speed and early rising:—but alas while we sat at dinner yesterday, old Rogers arrived,Samuel Rogers. TC means JWC, since Rogers was unmarried. like an assassinating Old Man of the Mountain;—assassinated this fair scheme: Breakfast with him, wife and I &c &c Ach Gott!
Take care of your cold, liebe Freundin; yes do, and don’t come back ill again,—I do not like that at all. And may the Divinities and Supreme Destinies of this world ever bless you.

div3.bibl:
Undated “Yes, my Lady; I am making ready to accompany”
Thomas Carlyle
Harriet Lady Ashburton >
TC HARRIET LADY ASHBURTON
div3.sourceNote: TC-LA, n.d. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: TC TO HARRIET LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: Yes, my Lady; I am making ready to accompany, this afternoon—lest I don’t see you again at all!
Shall expect you to pick me up at 4½ p.m.

div3.bibl:
Undated “The enclosed lay written since morning”
Thomas Carlyle
Harriet Lady Ashburton >
TC HARRIET LADY ASHBURTON
div3.sourceNote: TC-LA, n.d. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: TC TO HARRIET LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: The enclosed lay written since morning; but had not gone when your letter came. Am not I in luck? God, we are told, sends eat, and means of various kinds; but it is another Party that furnishes the Cooks! Let us not complain of anything.

There is bright lightning in the sky; there are brave days coming. I am very weary; in much haste,—accomplishing nothing. I send you my prayers if they availed aught. Good night, and peace be with you always.

div3.bibl:
Undated “Ma Dame—Mille Graces!”
Thomas Carlyle
Harriet Lady Ashburton >
TC HARRIET LADY ASHBURTON
div3.sourceNote: TC-LA, n.d. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: TC TO HARRIET LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: Ma Dame—Mille Graces! Sie sind schön und edel.“My Lady—a Thousand Blessings” (Fr.). “You are beautiful and noble” (Ger.). You make a bright hour wherever you come;—and not even Useful Knowledge and Orson the Cousin of ValentinePerhaps an allusion to the committee of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, on which served their mutual friend Charles Hay Cameron (1795–1880; ODNB), jurist. Characters from a Carolingian cycle romance about two brothers abandoned as children in the woods. Valentine is raised as a knight and Orson is raised in the den of a bear. Later, Valentine defeats and tames Orson. See TC to JAC, 20 Dec. 1831. can withstand you! The Cat is very happy.—
I will see you again, if it please Heaven, before long,—Sunday or some day. I have corrected my Proof-sheet; and end this day well.

closer.salute: I am yours to serve you evermore

div3.bibl:
Undated “I will call tomorrow about four o—clock”
Thomas Carlyle
Harriet Lady Ashburton >
TC HARRIET LADY ASHBURTON
div3.sourceNote: TC-LA, n.d. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. The clarity of TC’s handwriting suggests the letter is written to Harriet Lady Ashburton, but Louisa Lady Ashburton is also a possible recipient.
div3.head: TC TO HARRIET LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: I will call tomorrow about four o’clock; today I have missed it,—unhappy that I am! Pity me, be friendly to me, in your noble heart; her Majesty has no such subject as I,—in several unexpected respects, I do believe. God help us;—and bless you ever, Lady dear, befall what may!
docBody.ps:
Thursday (not 3 but 4 p.m.
(that is my mistake today)

div3.bibl:
Undated “You are the Queen of Women!”
Thomas Carlyle
Louisa Lady Ashburton >
TC LOUISA LADY ASHBURTON
div3.sourceNote: TC-LLA, n.d. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. K. J. Fielding acquired the copy of the text used here from Virginia Surtees and sent it to the Duke Letters Office in October 1981. On the typescript an editor posits “November?”
div3.head: TC TO LOUISA LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: You are the Queen of Women! Magnanimous, patient, gentle, brave and beautiful, beyond the Daughters of Eve. Oh, if I could fly away into Heaven with you,—would I!— The thought of you gilds all darknesses in my existence; makes wretched London fog itself into clouds of red and gold. Thanks, thanks, dear one.
docBody.ps: Saturday (an hour after you are gone).

div3.bibl:
Undated “If this is right, seal it and present it according to your benevolent intention”
Thomas Carlyle
Louisa Lady Ashburton >
TC LOUISA LADY ASHBURTON
div3.sourceNote: TC-LLA, n.d. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: TC TO LOUISA LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: If this is right, seal it and present it according to your benevolent intention,—and let us pray for a blessing on it.—I am near blind (so bilious &c &c) and have spent the whole morning, screwing out this wretched thing: it is very evident I shall never become eminent in the Diplomatic line, but must seek my promotion in some other,—out of this world, I believe at last!

I shall see you Saturday evening, from the distance: there is no chance of a Tea that will suit me again, till after your return from Paris?Harriet Lady Ashburton traveled to Paris in 1851 on 10 September (see JWC to KS, [22 Aug. 1851], and TC to JWC, 10 Sept. 1851), but this is not the correct trip because TC was in Scotland when she left for Paris in 1851. None, I suppose. That, as matters go, is almost my best resource; and Heaven knows it is not a very grand one.— Well, well!

There are some things beyond the reach of Tantalus and Zeus,While in Olympus at the invitation of Zeus, Tantalus stole ambrosia, the sacred food of the gods, and committed other crimes, for which he was sent to Tartarus, an abyss created to torment the wicked.—and be hanged to both of them!

closer.salute:
I will remain always (according to appearance)
Your noble Ladyship’s obedient

div3.bibl:
Undated “What is the use of collecting Autographs?”
Thomas Carlyle
An Autograph Hunter >
TC AN AUTOGRAPH HUNTER
div3.sourceNote: TC-LLA, n.d. MS: Sold at Sotheby’s, 27 May 1986. The description and quote are from the catalog entry.
div3.head: TC TO AN AUTOGRAPH HUNTER

docBody.p: Autograph sentiment for an autograph hunter: “What is the use of collecting Autographs? Endeavour to collect knowledge, wisdom and modest courage.” On a slip, c.4 by 5 inches. S May 27 (230) £130 [Maggs]

div3.bibl:
Undated “I was nearly killed last night”
Thomas Carlyle
W. H. Brookfield >
TC W. H. BROOKFIELD
div3.sourceNote: TC-WHB, n.d. MS: Gordon N. Ray. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: TC TO W. H. BROOKFIELD

docBody.p: Dear Brookfield,— I was nearly killed last night: if I dine again without pause— Good Heavens!
Well, if I possibly can or dare, I will nevertheless;—and unless you hear something from me about 4 p.m., expect me, you sinful being!

div3.bibl:
Undated “Euge! Same style of thing as the former”
Thomas Carlyle
Thomas Carlyle >
TC THOMAS CARLYLE
div3.sourceNote: TC-TC, n.d. MS: Representative Church Body Library, Dublin; RCB Library MS 253/2/16. Received by Hilary Smith from Raymond Refaussé, Librarian and archivist at the RCBL. TC’s note to himself may be referring to Henry Austin Bruce (1815–95; ODNB), politician.
div3.head: TC TO THOMAS CARLYLE

docBody.p: Euge!Lat. for “Bravo.” Same style of thing as the former.’ If Bruce cd only be awake to his own interest and his Country’s!— —

div3.bibl:
Undated “We cannot come to-morrow but there will another day arrive”
Thomas Carlyle
Julia Margaret Cameron >
TC [JULIA MARGARET CAMERON]
div3.sourceNote: TC-[JMC], n.d. [before 1867] Source: Maggs Brothers Catalogue, n.d., advertising the sale of a first edition of The French Revolution (1837) with a letter inserted. Although the catalog identifies the recipient as Charles Hay Cameron (1795–1880; ODNB), jurist, it is much more likely that the letter was sent to his wife, the photographer Julia Margaret Cameron, b. Pattle (1815–79; ODNB); see TC to LA, 14 Nov. 1851.
div3.head: TC TO [JULIA MARGARET CAMERON]

docBody.p: 119 CARLYLE (Thos.). The French Revolution: a History. First Edition. 3 vols., post 8vo, half calf gilt, s.e. London, 1837.

A fine copy, with all the half titles. Inserted is an Autograph Letter, 2 pp., signed by the author, to Mr. Cameron:—“ … We cannot come to-morrow but there will another day arrive (other days, with sun in them, and a studio nearer hand, and you shall have a stroke at my face if you persist in wishing it.Cameron took TC’s photograph in early June 1867, and TC described his face as “terrifically ugly and woe-begone”; see TC to JMC, 9 June 1867. Depend upon that, and let us (as the Latins say) ‘hasten slowly.’”The Lat. phrase is “Festina lente.”

div3.bibl:
Undated “You probably got my letter this morning in your way to Ecclefechan Station?”
Thomas Carlyle
John Aitken Carlyle >
TC JOHN AITKEN CARLYLE
div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, n.d. [1842 or after]. MS: Hornel Collection, #22, Broughton House, Kirkcudbright. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN AITKEN CARLYLE

docBody.p: Dear Brother,— You probably got my letter this morning in your way to Ecclefechan Station?

I only wish to say that, if you find no bed at your old Lodgings, of course there is a bed for you at your Brother’s house,—under the old (saddish) conditions! Your welcome, from me, so long as I have a house in this world, is always sure.
docBody.ps:
I write this at Bath House,The London home of Lord and Lady Ashburton. TC was not a frequent guest there until 1842. in the utmost haste.
Tuesday, 4½ p.m.

div3.bibl:
Undated “I find I shall need 8 copies of that Book”
Thomas Carlyle
Chapman and Hall’s Clerk
>
TC [CHAPMAN AND HALL’S CLERK]
div3.sourceNote: TC-[CAHC], n.d. [before June 1870]. MS: Hornel Collection, #22, Broughton House, Kirkcudbright. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: TC TO [CHAPMAN AND HALL’S CLERK]

docBody.p: Dear Sir,
I find I shall still need 8 copies of that Book: will you have the goodness to send them to me as soon as possible.

I hope Forster and DickensJohn Forster (1812–76; ODNB) and Charles Dickens (1812–70; ODNB. were naturally each supplied with a copy: if not, pray let the omission be straightway rectified;—or if it be not yet too late, I could write my name on each of the two copies if I had them here.

div3.bibl:
Undated “This man ‘Henry Hudson’ seems to be mad”
Thomas Carlyle
Chapman and Hall’s Clerk
>
TC CHAPMAN AND HALL’S CLERK
div3.sourceNote: TC-[CAHC], 27 July, n.y.. MS: Strouse. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: TC TO CHAPMAN AND HALL’S CLERK

docBody.p: This man ‘Henry Hudson’Perhaps the same person mentioned in JWC to JBUL, 19 March 1865, and TC to EWA, 13 July 1865. seems to be mad: keep that second Note of his as a specimen, and refuse any other that may come in the same hand
To Mr Chapman’s Clerk

div3.bibl:
Undated “Much to my regret I must not think of coming!”
Thomas Carlyle
Derwent Coleridge >
TC DERWENT COLERIDGE
div3.sourceNote: TC-DCO, n.d. [before 1864]. MS: NLS Acc. 9655. Derwent Coleridge (1800–1883; ODNB), writer and educationist, principal of St. Mark’s College, Chelsea (1841–64). The son of the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834; ODNB), he m., 6 Dec. 1827, Mary Simpson Pridham (1807–87). The response to is invitation was probably written before 1864, when Coleridge became rector at Hanwell, Middlesex.
div3.head: TC TO DERWENT COLERIDGE

docBody.p: My Dear Sir,

Much to my regret I must not think of coming! I am verging towards the end of a most horrible Task (scribble-scribbling) and for these many weeks have had to deny myself all cheerful meeting of symposial friends,—often, one might say, all paths of articulate-speaking men! In a month or less I hope to be at large again, and see you all.

closer.salute:
With very kind regards to Mrs. Coleridge,
Yours always truly
